title: Al-Aqsa in Jerusalem
hookLine: the farthest mosque in Jerusalem, named third in the hadith of the three mosques

lines: THE GOLD DOME IS THE SHRINE.
THE ROWS FORM AT THE FAR END.
cards: On a wide stone platform in the Old City of Jerusalem, two buildings catch the light. One wears a golden dome: the Dome of the Rock, a shrine built over the rock, which we met months back.

The other is lower and longer, at the southern end, under a plainer gray dome. The gold steals the eye. But the long building is where the rows form on a Friday, shoulder to shoulder, facing south toward Mecca.
Its name comes straight out of a verse of the Qur'an. Today: Al-Aqsa in Jerusalem.

teach.h: THE FAR DISTANT PLACE OF WORSHIP.
teach.b: Start with the verse. Surah seventeen opens with the Night Journey of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him.
In Pickthall's translation, God carried His servant by night "from the Inviolable Place of Worship to the Far Distant Place of Worship." The Inviolable one is the mosque in Mecca.
The Far Distant one, in Arabic al-masjid al-aqsa, is the farthest mosque, and the verse gave the place its name. Notice what it leaves out: it never names Jerusalem.
Muslims have understood the Far Distant place as the mosque there. Second, the list from two days ago.
A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says not to set out on a special journey except to three mosques: the Sacred Mosque in Mecca, the Prophet's own mosque in Medina, and al-Aqsa.
Jerusalem is named third, and this week has walked them in that order. Third, an older link. In another hadith, a companion, Abu Dharr, asked which mosque was set up first on earth.
The answer: the Sacred Mosque. And then? Al-Aqsa.

teach.h: PAIRED WITH MECCA FROM THE START.
teach.b: The two are paired from the start. Fourth, the name stretches.

teach.h: A HALL, OR THE WHOLE SANCTUARY.
teach.b: Some use al-Aqsa for the long prayer hall alone; others for the whole walled enclosure, courtyards, trees, the Dome of the Rock and all, also called the Noble Sanctuary.
The same hill is holy to Jews, who call it the Temple Mount, and the city is dear to Christians. A crowded holiness, and a reason people of more than one faith pray for its peace.

how: Muslims who can travel to Jerusalem often pray at al-Aqsa, and those who cannot remember it in their prayers and in the story of the Night Journey, recited from Surah al-Isra.

games.q: you're Abu Dharr. you've asked the Prophet which mosque was set up first on earth, and he's told you: the Sacred Mosque. what do you ask next?
games.why: he asks "and then which?" and the answer is al-Aqsa. in the hadith the two are paired from the start.

practice: Hold Jerusalem in mind as a place, not a headline: stone streets, bells and calls to prayer, families buying bread, children on their way to school, worshippers of more than one faith passing in the same lanes.
If you pray, ask in your own words for peace and safety for the city and everyone who lives there; if you don't, simply wish them well, one face at a time.
